personalEssay.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?
personalEssay.text:
When my nani moved in with us from Karachi, I was twelve and I was annoyed. She took over my bedroom. She watched Pakistani dramas at full volume. And she had opinions about everything, from how I wore my hair to the fact that I answered her in English when she spoke to me in Urdu.

I want to be honest: I was not a good granddaughter that first year. I stayed in my room, which was now the garage-turned-office my dad had cleared out for me, and I pretended not to hear her when she called my name. My Urdu was the kind you use to ask for more roti. I couldn't have a real conversation with her, and I didn't want to try.

The thing that changed us was a poem.

It was during Ramadan, the year I turned thirteen. I couldn't sleep after suhoor, and I came into the kitchen and found her sitting at the table with an old book, reading out loud to herself. She was reciting Ghalib, the nineteenth-century poet, in a low, rhythmic voice. I didn't understand most of the words. But I understood that she was crying a little, and that she wasn't sad exactly.

I asked her what it meant. She looked surprised, like she'd forgotten I could be interested in anything. Then she patted the chair next to her and said, "Baith. I'll teach you."

My nani says a ghazal is a conversation with someone who isn't in the room. Every couplet stands on its own, but they all circle the same ache. That first night she explained one couplet for almost an hour, word by word, the double meanings, the way a single image could mean love and God and grief at the same time. I went back to bed at five in the morning, and for the first time, I was the one who wanted to keep talking.

After that, we read together almost every night. Ghalib, Mir, Faiz. She taught me the meters by tapping them on the table. She corrected my pronunciation constantly and without mercy. Slowly, my Urdu stopped being kitchen Urdu. I started understanding the dramas she watched. I started arguing with her, in Urdu, about whether Faiz was a better poet than Ghalib. (He isn't, according to her. I disagree.)

What surprised me most was what she gave me without meaning to. I had always felt split in two: American at school, Pakistani at home, and not fully either. But in those poems, I found a part of myself that was older than both. A whole tradition of people writing about longing and exile and faith, who would have understood exactly what it felt like to live between two places.

That changed how I write, too. I'd been writing poetry in English since middle school, mostly bad poems about my feelings. After I started reading ghazals with my nani, my poems got stranger and better. I started borrowing the forms, the repeated rhyme, the way each couplet turns. One of those poems won a Silver Key last year. I read it to her first. She said the rhyme in the fourth couplet was weak. She was right.

My nani is eighty-one now, and her eyes are getting worse, so now I'm the one who reads to her. Some nights she falls asleep halfway through a ghazal. I always finish it anyway, out loud, to the room.

I didn't know when I was twelve that the person taking over my bedroom was about to give me a language, a tradition, and a version of myself I didn't know was there. I'm still thanking her, one couplet at a time.

supplements.prompt: Amherst's open curriculum lets students design their own course of study. What do you hope to explore, and why?
supplements.text:
I want to explore what happens to a poem when it crosses a border.

My grandmother taught me to read classical Urdu poetry when I was thirteen, sitting at our kitchen table in Las Vegas at four in the morning during Ramadan. My nani says a ghazal is a conversation with someone who isn't in the room. Every couplet stands on its own, but they all circle the same ache. Since then I've become obsessed with translation: how you carry a poem from Urdu into English without losing what makes it alive. Most English translations of Ghalib I've read are either beautiful and inaccurate or accurate and boring. I want to figure out whether there's a third way.

Amherst's open curriculum is the reason I'm applying. I don't want to choose between English, comparative literature, Asian languages, and religion. I want to take all of them and let them run into each other. I'd love to take courses in literary translation and the history of South Asia, and maybe learn Persian, since so much Urdu poetry comes from it.

I also love the idea of working on a literary magazine with other students who care about language. As the magazine's managing editor this year, I added a section for poems in translation at my school, and our twenty-person staff voted it the best part of each issue. I'd love to do something like that at Amherst, maybe a bilingual reading series.

In the long run, I want to become a translator and a poet, and maybe a teacher. I want to help readers in English meet poets like Ghalib and Faiz the way I did: slowly, word by word, with someone patient sitting next to them.
